analysis.one_liner: Creates a low-cost government-run health plan that anyone can buy on the ACA exchanges.
analysis.headline: The Medicare-X Choice Act, a public health insurance option with 14 House Democratic sponsors, never received a hearing, committee vote, or floor vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set up a 'Medicare Exchange health plan' — a government-administered insurance plan sold alongside private plans on the ACA marketplaces, starting in a few areas and nationwide by 2025. It would pay doctors and hospitals Medicare rates (which are lower than commercial rates), require most Medicare and Medicaid providers to accept it, and cover primary care with no copays. It would also raise federal subsidies for marketplace coverage, remove the income cap that cut off help above four times the poverty level, fix the 'family glitch' that denied subsidies to spouses and children, and lift the ban on Medicare negotiating drug prices.
analysis.who_benefits: People buying insurance on their own or through small employers — especially in areas where only one insurer offers plans or where prices are high — would get a lower-priced public alternative. Middle-income households earning above 400% of the poverty line, who today get no premium subsidies, would become eligible. Spouses and children priced out of employer coverage under the 'family glitch' could get marketplace subsidies instead. Medicare beneficiaries would eventually benefit if the government's new authority to negotiate drug prices lowered prices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Marketplace customers, the uninsured, middle-income families

how_it_helps.text: Creates a government-administered plan sold on the individual and small-group exchanges, phased in nationwide for individuals by plan year 2025, with priority for areas where only one insurer offers plans or where provider shortages keep prices high.
Reimburses providers at Medicare rates and lets providers in rural areas be paid up to 50% more, so the plan's premiums can stay low and the plan can compete on price.
Covers primary care services with no cost-sharing at all.

Requires providers enrolled in Medicare or a state Medicaid plan to participate in the plan unless they qualify for a narrow opt-out when participation would threaten their ability to operate, so enrollees would have broad provider access.

Expands premium tax credits by removing the 400%-of-poverty income cap and fixes the 'family glitch', letting family members get subsidies when employer family coverage costs more than 9.5% of household income.

Strikes the statutory restriction (section 1860D-11(i)) that barred the Health Secretary from interfering with private drug-plan negotiations, giving HHS authority to negotiate Medicare prescription drug prices.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would fund $1 billion to launch the plan, $1 billion for data and technology, $10 billion a year in fiscal 2022-2024 for nationwide reinsurance that lowers premiums, and the expanded tax credits. Hospitals and doctors would earn Medicare rates — lower than commercial insurance rates — on a growing share of patients. Private insurers would lose enrollment to the public plan.

drawbacks.text: Providers paid Medicare rates instead of commercial rates would see revenue fall, and because doctors cannot turn away the plan's patients except in exceptional circumstances, some medical practices could face real financial pressure — the narrow opt-out is the bill's most contested feature.

The plan's premiums must cover its full actuarial cost, but a cheaper Medicare-rate plan could attract healthier customers away from private plans, raising premiums for everyone left in the private risk pool.
The bill authorizes substantial new federal spending: $2 billion in startup funds, $10 billion per year for reinsurance in fiscal 2022-2024, and higher tax-credit costs from lifting the income cap.
Small-government critics object on principle to the federal government running an insurance plan that competes directly with private companies.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people who struggle to afford coverage — especially in one-insurer markets and in middle-income households shut out of subsidies — the benefits are large and concrete: a cheaper plan option, free primary care, and broader subsidies. The real costs fall on specific groups: hospitals and doctors taking Medicare-level payments, private insurers losing enrollment, and taxpayers funding roughly $32 billion of reinsurance and startup funding plus the subsidy expansion. The provider-participation mandate is aggressive and would be the hardest thing to negotiate; without it, the plan would have thin networks, but with it, some providers would face sharp payment cuts.

outcome.mechanism: Referred to two House committees and a Health subcommittee on the day it was introduced, the bill never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Antonio Delgado (D-NY) introduced the Medicare-X Choice Act of 2021 on February 23, 2021, joined by Reps. Brian Higgins (D-NY) and John Larson (D-CT).
The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees the same day, and then to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee on February 24, 2021.
Thirteen House members cosponsored the bill, all Democrats; no Republican cosponsor joined.
The action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote at any point after the initial referral, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private insurers, hospital systems, and drug manufacturers are better off because the bill died: the government did not gain a seat in the insurance market, providers kept commercial payment rates, and Medicare still cannot negotiate drug prices. People paying high marketplace premiums, and middle-income families excluded from subsidies, got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private insurers, hospital systems, drug makers

sides.party_line_note: All 14 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats, and no Republican ever cosponsored; the bill's fate, however, was decided in committee under Democratic control rather than by a floor vote.

industries.note: A government plan paying Medicare rates would undercut private marketplace plans on price, and the bill prioritizes it for markets where insurers face little competition. The bill's reinsurance fund and expanded subsidies would bring insurers more customers and lower-cost pools, but the core competition effect is a loss of enrollment and pricing power.

Providers would be paid Medicare rates, which are well below commercial rates, on all plan patients, and Medicare and Medicaid enrollment would effectively require accepting the plan — with an opt-out only where participation would threaten the practice's survival. Lower payments would squeeze provider revenue, particularly for practices dependent on privately insured patients.

The bill strikes the statute barring HHS from negotiating Medicare drug prices, opening the door to government-set prices for the first time. Lower negotiated drug prices would eventually flow to Medicare beneficiaries but cut into manufacturers' revenue.

industries.industry: Community health organizations and higher education institutions
industries.note: The bill authorizes grants to universities, local education agencies, nonprofits, and health agencies for community health partnerships and shared data systems. This is a modest funding stream alongside the plan's main provisions.
